title: Agrippa and the Three Books of Occult Philosophy
otherNames: De occulta philosophia libri tres (Latin title, 1533)
Three Books of Occult Philosophy (J.F.'s English, 1651)
Of Occult Philosophy, or of Magick (1651 running title)
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim; 'Henry Cornelius Agrippa' in the English editions
family: source book: the Renaissance compendium that carried most of the wing's alphabets into print
summary: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486-1535) wrote De occulta philosophia as a young man and sent the draft to Abbot Trithemius, who replied on 8 April 1510. He printed Book I in 1531 and the three books, much enlarged, in July 1533. In between (1530) he published a declamation on the vanity of the sciences in which he retracted the work. The books follow his three worlds: Book I natural (elemental), Book II celestial, Book III ceremonial (intellectual). Characters appear at each level, but the full magical alphabets (the Honorian 'Theban' in III.29; Celestial, Malachim and Passing the River in III.30) sit in Book III, because Agrippa classes them as the writings of spirits and sacred things. The 'Fourth Book' printed under his name after his death is spurious. The standard English is J.F.'s of 1651.

firstAttestation.locator: 1651 English: Trithemius's reply and Agrippa's letter in the front matter; Book I ends p. 163; Book II pp. 165-340; Book III pp. 341-556; letters pp. 557-566; Censure pp. 567-583; colophon after the Censure.
firstAttestation.notes: The 1510 text differs from the print. Agrippa says so himself: in 1527 the first two books were 'dificient in many things' and the third 'wholy imperfect'; in 1531 he had 'added many things to many Chapters'. So no chapter of Books II-III, including the alphabets, should be dated 1510 or 1531 without the manuscript. Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Leiden: Brill, 1992), which reports the early redaction, was not consulted. Printers of the 1531 Book I (Antwerp: Joannes Grapheus; Paris: Christian Wechel) are recalled, not verified. The sibling celestial file lists Paris, Antwerp and Cologne printings of 1531.

It also holds Agrippa's printing of the Honorian alphabet (III.29), which Trithemius had printed first, in 1518. The sibling catalogues record four or five issues. As recalled from Nauert (1965), the printing ran into opposition from the Cologne inquisitor Conrad Köllin; not checked here.

claims.claim: Agrippa wrote De occulta philosophia for Trithemius in 1510.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's dedicatory letter and Trithemius's reply dated 8 April 1510, printed in the 1533 front matter (1651 English). The draft is also described in 'To the Reader'.

Agrippa himself says it is not. In 1527 the third book was 'wholy imperfect ... a certain Epitome'. In January 1531 he had 'inserted many things in many places, and ... added many things to many Chapters'. 'To the Reader' (1533) says 'we added some Chapters'. Which chapters were added can only be settled from the Würzburg manuscript or Perrone Compagni 1992.
sources: J.F. 1651, EEBO-TCP A26565, front matter and letters (pp. 557-559)

claims.claim: The Celestial, Malachim, Passing the River and nine-chamber systems, the planetary seals and the Honorian alphabet go back to Agrippa's 1510 draft (or to 1531).
claims.evidence: No evidence found. The 1531 printing was Book I only, which holds none of them. Whether the draft contains them is unchecked. Use 1533.
sources: sibling research files celestial, malachim, theban, planetary-seals, aiq-bekar
J.F. 1651 (Book II dedication: Book I published first)

claims.claim: Book I was printed on its own in 1531.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's Book I dedication is dated Mechelen, January 1531. The Book II dedication says he promised the rest 'when I published the first of them'. The printers (Antwerp: Grapheus; Paris: Wechel) are recalled, and the sibling celestial file also names Cologne.

claims.claim: The complete edition appeared at Cologne in July 1533, printed by Johannes Soter.
claims.evidence: July 1533 is secure: the colophon is recorded in the Utrecht and Eton catalogues (sibling research) and translated at the end of the 1651 volume. The place and printer are unsigned: Eton gives '[J. Soter?]' and notes Adams's suggestion of Basel.

claims.claim: Agrippa recanted De occulta philosophia in De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum (1530).
claims.evidence: The recantation sentence appears in the 1676 English of De vanitate (ch. XLVIII) and in the 'Censure' printed with the three books (1651). 'To the Reader' (1533) says he 'did for the most part retract this book'. Whether it was sincere, prudent or rhetorical is argued in the scholarship (the site names Nauert, Zambelli and van der Poel) and is not settled.
sources: EEBO-TCP A26565 (1651), pp. 567-583 and front matter

claims.claim: The three books map onto three worlds: elemental, celestial and intellectual.
claims.evidence: I.1: 'a three f[o]ld World. Elementary, Celestiall, and intellectuall'; 'the first contains naturall Magick, the second Celestiall, and the third Ceremoniall'.

claims.claim: Characters are treated at three levels, and the alphabets of spirits belong in Book III.
claims.evidence: The arrangement is Agrippa's. Natural characters stamped by stars come in I.33. Celestial characters (geomantic, by likeness, Hermes's star characters) come in II.51-52, with a forward reference from the Malachim in II.51: 'But of these hereafter'. The 'Characters and Seals of spirits', the Hebrew scripts and revealed signs come in III.29-31. Calling this a three-tier theory is my reading of that arrangement.

claims.claim: Agrippa invented the Celestial, Malachim, Passing the River and Theban alphabets.
claims.evidence: He claims none of them. He gives the Honorian alphabet as one 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes' (III.29). He gives the other three as writings found 'amongst the Hebrews' (III.30) and the nine chambers as 'delivered by Cabalists'. Trithemius had printed the Honorian alphabet in 1518, and de Balmes a 'beyond the river' script in 1523 (siblings).

claims.claim: Agrippa taught that characters compel spirits.
claims.evidence: In III.30 he says the opposite of angels: by the marks we consecrate to them 'we cannot any way compel them to us, but by which we rise up to them'. Elsewhere he reports pagan beliefs about compulsion (III.31, Porphyry and Iamblichus) and treats the 'bonds of spirits' (III.33). Do not summarise his position as compulsion.

claims.claim: Agrippa shows how to draw the planetary seals from the magic squares.
claims.evidence: No. II.22 says the method is for 'the wise searcher ... [to] easily find out'. Modern construction rules are reconstructions.

claims.claim: Hebrew is the language of the angels.
claims.evidence: Agrippa reports it: 'many think that if they use any Idiome, it is Hebrew' (III.23). He calls Hebrew letters 'the most efficacious of all' (I.74), and the names of God must stay 'in their own Characters' (III.11).

claims.claim: The square Hebrew letters were instituted by Ezra; Moses used an older script.
claims.evidence: Agrippa states it in III.30, and De vanitate ch. 2 repeats it with the rabbinic disagreements. It is a traditional view, reported as Agrippa's. For the history of the scripts, see the Hebrew and Phoenician halls.

claims.claim: The 'Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy' is by Agrippa.
claims.evidence: Rejected by Johann Weyer, his former famulus (De praestigiis daemonum, 1563, as the site's Latin hall states). Turner (1655) nonetheless printed it as Agrippa's. Its opening claims to be the 'Complement and Key' of the three books, echoing Agrippa's 1527 promise of a 'key' for intimate friends. Scholarship treats it as spurious.

The EEBO-TCP catalogue: 'The translator is probably John French. Cf. DNB' (authority heading French, John, 1616-1657). The Wellcome record gives John French or John Freake (sibling). Tyson's edition, as recalled, names 'James Freake'. Peterson argues for French (sibling celestial). The site's Powers texts call it 'the 1651 Freake translation'; change that to 'J.F.'s translation (1651)'.
The documents show a stay at Würzburg, conversations, the dedication and one reply in which Trithemius praises and advises. 'Teacher' or 'master' goes beyond them.

claims.claim: The 'most elegant marks of numbers' in II.19 are the medieval Cistercian ciphers.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's rule (tens by turning to the left, hundreds and thousands by turning downwards) is the cipher rule. King (2001) treats Agrippa's printing as a witness (recalled). Agrippa only says he found them in 'two most ancient books of Astrologers, and Magicians'.
sources: David A. King, The Ciphers of the Monks (Stuttgart, 2001), recalled

letters.name: Front matter: 'To the Reader'; Agrippa's letter to Trithemius and Trithemius's reply; dedication to Hermann von Wied
letters.form: Not a glyph. A text card with three dated documents: (1) Trithemius's reply, dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (the abbey of St Jakob, Würzburg); (2) the dedication of Book I to Hermann von Wied, archbishop of Cologne, dated 'From Mechlinia, Anno M. D. XXXI. In the moneth of January' (Mechelen, January 1531); (3) 'To the Reader', in which Agrippa says he gave the youthful draft to Trithemius, that it circulated 'imperfect' in Italy, France and Germany, that he added chapters for the print, and that he had 'for the most part' retracted it in his book on the vanity of the sciences.
letters.note: Dates and wording are from the 1651 English as keyed by EEBO-TCP. J.F.'s 'Neapolitanian' is evidently a slip for the Latin Peapolitanus/Herbipolis (Würzburg); his own text of Trithemius's letter has 'Peapolis' and Agrippa's letter has 'Herbipolis'. Agrippa's letter to Trithemius carries no date in the 1651 text.
letters.sentence: I confess whilst I was very yong, I set upon the writing of these books, but hoping that I should set them forth with corrections and enlargements, and for that cause I gave them to Tritemius a Neapolitanian Abbot, formerly a Spanhemensian, a man very industrious after secret things.

letters.name: I.1 How Magicians Collect vertues from the three-fold World, is declared in these three Books
letters.form: Not a glyph. A diagram card: three stacked bands, Elementary (Book I, natural magic), Celestial (Book II, celestial magic), Intellectual (Book III, ceremonial magic), with an arrow descending (virtues sent down from God through angels, heavens, stars, elements) and an arrow ascending (the magician's ascent 'by the same degrees through each World'). Place the wing's chapters on the bands (see lettersSource).
letters.note: The chapter's opening names the worlds: 'a three f[o]ld World. Elementary, Celestiall, and intellectuall' (TCP has an illegible letter in 'fold'). The mapping world = book is Agrippa's own (I.1); the 1651 verse encomium by 'Eugenius Philalethes' ends 'But his Three Books with the Three worlds shall stand.' (Eugenius Philalethes is generally identified as Thomas Vaughan; recalled, not checked.)
letters.sentence: The order and process of all these I shall endeavor to deliver in these three Books: Whereof the first contains naturall Magick, the second Celestiall, and the third Ceremoniall.

letters.name: I.33 Of the Seals, and Characters of Naturall things
letters.form: Card with the heading, the sentence, and seven small panels: 'The Letters, or Characters' of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury and the Moon, said to be the signs chiromancers read in the hand. The figures are woodcuts that EEBO-TCP did not key ([FIGURE] only), so nothing here describes their strokes. Trace from the 1533 (Library of Congress copy) or 1651 scan, or omit the panels.
letters.note: Natural characters: stars 'stamp' a seal or character on stones, plants, animals and the human hand. This is the first, lowest tier of Agrippa's theory of characters (Book I = elemental world). Sibling item signs-of-the-art treats the planetary signs themselves.

letters.name: I.70 Of the vertue of proper names
letters.form: Not a glyph. Text card. Pair it with I.69 (speech), I.71 (sentences, verses, charms) and I.72 (enchantments), which complete Agrippa's natural theory of the spoken word before he reaches writing (I.73) and letters (I.74).
letters.note: The chapter grounds the power of names in Adam's naming of creatures (Genesis 2) and reports Apollonius reviving a girl after learning her name (from Philostratus). Reported, not endorsed.
letters.sentence: Hence Magicians say, that proper names of things are certain rayes of things, every where present at all times, keeping the power of things, as the essence of the thing signified, rules, and is discerned in them, and know the things by them, as by proper, and living Images.

letters.name: I.73 Of the vertue of writting, and of making imprecations, and inscriptions
letters.form: Not a glyph. Text card; the chapter has no figures.
letters.note: Agrippa adds that 'Magicians command, that in every work, there be imprecations, and inscriptions made', citing Albertus's Speculum and Virgil's eighth Eclogue. This is the hinge from speech to letters.
letters.sentence: Now writing is the last expression of the mind, and is the number of speech and voice, as also the collection, state, end, continuing, and iteration, making a habit, which is not perfected with the act of ones voice.

letters.name: I.74 Of the proportion, correspondency, reduction of Letters to the Celestiall Signs, and Planets, according to various tongues, with a Table shewing this
letters.translit: J.F. 1651, pp. 160-163, plus a folding table
letters.form: Card with the sentence and a correspondence table built from the text, not from the plate: HEBREW 22 letters = 3 mothers (elements: fire, water, earth; 'they account Aire no Element') + 7 doubles (planets) + 12 simples (signs); GREEK 7 vowels = planets, 12 consonants = signs, the other 5 = four elements and the spirit of the world; LATIN A E I O U with consonantal J and V = 7 planets, B C D F G L M N P R S T = 12 signs, K Q X Z = 4 elements, H = spirit of the world, Y follows Greek. The printed table itself (a fold-out in 1651, keyed by TCP only as 'Place this Table after folio [illegible]') was not seen; per II.19 it also carries a 'Chaldean' alphabet. Do not draw that alphabet without a scan.
letters.note: The Latin and Greek groupings above are copied from the 1651 text (the Greek letters themselves are not keyed by TCP). The 3/7/12 division is the Sefer Yetzirah scheme, which Agrippa gives as the teaching of 'the masters of the Hebrews' without naming the book. Also from this chapter: 'There are therefore two and twenty Letters, which are the foundation of the world ...'. The house Latin hall already warns that such Latin tables are sixteenth-century constructions, not Roman inheritance.
letters.sentence: But before all notes of languages, the writing of the Hebrews is of all the most sacred in the figures of Characters, points of vowels, and tops of accents, as consisting in matter, form, and spirit.

letters.name: II.19 Of the notes of the Hebrews, and Caldeans, and certain other notes of Magicians
letters.form: Two panels. (a) Hebrew letter-numerals, keyed by TCP in full: units א-ט 1-9, tens י-צ 10-90, hundreds ק ר ש ת 100-400 and the five finals ך ם ן ף ץ 500-900; thousands by a 'great Character' (א = 1000); the alternative without finals (תק 500 ... תתק 900); fifteen written as nine and six, not ten and five, 'out of honor to the divine name' (TCP does not key that Hebrew; the standard form is ט״ו). (b) 'certain most elegant marks of numbers' from 'two most ancient books of Astrologers, and Magicians': base signs for 1-9; the same 'turned to the left hand' make tens; marks 'turned downwards' on the right hand make hundreds, and on the left thousands; compounded examples 1510, 1511, 1471, 1486, 2421. TCP did not key these signs, so their strokes are NOT DESCRIBED here.
letters.note: The rule for the magicians' marks (units, tens by left turn, hundreds and thousands by downward turns) is the rule of the medieval 'ciphers of the monks'; David A. King, The Ciphers of the Monks (Stuttgart: Steiner, 2001) treats Agrippa's printing among its witnesses (recalled, not checked this session). The Hebrew forms in panel (a) were drawn from the TCP keying, which gives the Hebrew in Unicode here. Agrippa also says 'We have set down their [the Chaldeans'] Alphabet in the end of the first book', i.e. the I.74 table.
letters.sentence: Moreover I found in two most ancient books of Astrologers, and Magicians, certain most elegant marks of numbers, which I thought good to set down in this place;

letters.name: II.20 What numbers are attributed to letters; and of divining by the same
letters.form: A number table for the Latin alphabet, as the 1651 text prints it: A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4, E 5, F 6, G 7, H 8, I 9, K 10, L 20, M 30, N 40, O 50, P 60, Q 70, R 80, S 90, T 100, V 200, X 300, Y 400, Z 500, I [consonant J] 600, V [consonant] 700, HI 800, HV 900. Then the rule: sum the letters of a person's name and both parents' names, cast out nines (remainder 1 or 4 Sun, 2 or 7 Moon, 3 Jupiter, 5 Mercury, 6 Venus, 8 Saturn, 9 Mars), or cast out twelves for the 'horoscope'.
letters.note: Agrippa ascribes the method to 'Alexandrinus the Philosopher' and calls it arithmancy. The values are directly usable by the wing's transliterator as 'Agrippa's Latin numbers'. Label them as Agrippa's scheme, not as Roman practice.
letters.sentence: The Pythagorians say (Aristotle, and Ptolemy are of opinion) that the very Elements of letters have some certain divine numbers, by which collected from proper names of things, we may draw conjectures concerning occult things to come.

letters.name: II.22 Of the tables of the Planets, their vertues, forms, and what Divine names, Intelligencies, and Spirits are set over them
letters.form: Not drawn here; reuse the sibling item planetary-seals. For the card: seven squares (Saturn 3x3 ... Moon 9x9), each printed 'in his compass' in Arabic figures and again 'In Hebrew notes', with the divine names, the Intelligence and the Spirit of each planet and their seals. Checked by script against the TCP keying: the 1651 Saturn, Jupiter, Mars and Sun squares agree cell for cell with the sibling's layouts. The Venus, Mercury and Moon squares do not. Several cells are swapped or misprinted in the 1651 print as keyed, which its errata partly correct, and TCP marks some cells illegible.
letters.note: Agrippa does not explain how the seals are drawn from the squares; he leaves it to 'the wise searcher'. Any page that shows a construction method must say it is a modern reconstruction. lettersSource: NOT AN ALPHABET. The units are the 25 parts of De occulta philosophia that a reader of this wing should know: 23 chapters plus the front matter and the end-matter Censure. Each has its 1651 heading, its book and chapter number (Perrone Compagni/1533 numbering, the same as the chapter's position in the 1651 volume), the 1651 pages, a card description in 'form', and one exact sentence ('sentence') from J.F.'s 1651 English as keyed by EEBO-TCP A26565 (CC0). Every quotation in this file was checked by script against the TCP text (A26565; A26562 for Turner 1655; A26566 for the 1676 Vanity). The check ignores case; display capitals and the long s are normalised. CHAPTER COUNT, checked in TCP: Book I 74, Book II 60, Book III 65 chapters. The 1651 misprints three headings in Book II: position 14 is headed 'XIII' (Of eleven and twelve), 16 'XIV' (notes of numbers in gestures), 17 'XVI' (Roman notes). Cite those as II.14, II.16, II.17. CHECKED BUT LEFT OUT: I.69, I.71, I.72 (speech, verses, enchantments); II.21; III.2 (secrecy); III.28 (names from things); III.32-33 (calling and binding spirits). FIGURES: TCP keys no woodcut ([FIGURE] only) and gives no Greek and almost no Hebrew. So no glyph is described from this file; the glyphs belong to the sibling items (theban, celestial, malachim, transitus-fluvii, aiq-bekar, planetary-seals, signs-of-the-art). The Hebrew numerals in II.19 are the exception: TCP keys them.

links.relation: III.29 prints the Honorian alphabet 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes'. Agrippa never uses the word 'Theban'.
III.30, 1651 p. 440. II.51 calls the Malachim 'the writing of Angels' and points forward to it.
III.30: the twenty-seven letters in nine chambers and the Michael example.
II.22: squares, names, intelligences, spirits and seals. Agrippa withholds the seal construction.
I.33 (chiromantic planetary letters), II.48 (geomantic figures), II.51 (characters from geomantic figures), II.52 (signs by likeness; Hermes's Behenian star characters).
Front matter: Agrippa's dedication and Trithemius's reply of 8 April 1510. III.24 cites Trithemius's treatise to Maximilian on the seven governing spirits.
III.29 defines characters as 'unknowable letters ... which the Ancients called Hyeroglyphicall, or sacred letters'. III.31 adds Porphyry on signs and images.
Absent from Agrippa: neither the 1651 text nor Turner's 1655 Fourth Book mentions Paracelsus or an 'alphabet of the Magi'.

I.74 (22 letters; 3 mothers, 7 doubles, 12 simples), II.19 (letter-numerals and finals), III.11 and III.25 (notariqon, gematria, Ziruph, the 72 names), III.23 (Hebrew as angelic speech, reported), III.30 (Mosaic script vs. Ezra's letters).
I.74 assigns Latin letters to planets, signs and elements; II.20 numbers the Latin alphabet 1-900. Both are Agrippa's constructions, as the Latin hall already warns.
I.74: Greek vowels to the seven planets, twelve consonants to the signs, five to the elements and spirit. II.18 covers the Greek numerals.
III.30: joined-letter characters 'most received' among the Arabians. III.26 and III.27 cite Arabian methods; the Censure cites Picatrix.
III.11 Abracadabra (Serenus Sammonicus); III.29 hieroglyphic sacred letters (Porphyry); III.31 Hecate's oracle (Porphyry). These are late-antique sources quoted by Agrippa.
De vanitate ch. 2 (1530; 1676 English) on Phoenician letters brought to Greece by Linus and Cadmus. Agrippa's sceptical counterpart to I.74.
De vanitate ch. 2 counts Syriac among the 'seven sorts of Letters most famous in Antiquity'.

cautions: Date Book II and Book III material (all the alphabets, the squares and seals, the nine chambers) to 1533, not 1510 (the draft) or 1531 (Book I only).

Cite chapters by book and position (II.22, III.29, III.30 and so on). These match Perrone Compagni/1533 and the order of the 1651 volume. The 1651 misprints three Book II headings (positions 14, 16, 17 headed XIII, XIV, XVI).

Attribute every alphabet as Agrippa does: the Honorian to Peter of Abano's report of Honorius (III.29); the Celestial, Malachim and Passing the River to 'the Hebrews'; the nine chambers to 'Cabalists'. Never write 'Agrippa's alphabet' as if he invented it.
The Fourth Book (1559, or 1565 per the NUC) is not Agrippa's. Its 'characters of good and evil spirits', made of 'lines and heads', must not be shown as Agrippa's.

Call the 1651 translator 'J.F.' and give both identifications (John French, probably, per EEBO-TCP/DNB; Freake per Tyson and others). The site's 'Freake translation' (src/data/powers/texts.js) should be softened.
The 'Censure' and De vanitate passages on Kabbalah contain anti-Jewish polemic. Quote the recantation sentence, not the polemic, and frame anything quoted as Agrippa's 1530 polemic.

EEBO-TCP keys no figures, no Greek and almost no Hebrew (the II.19 numerals are the exception), and has illegible letters in III.10, III.11 and II.22. All glyphs and Hebrew spellings must come from a scan (1533 Library of Congress copy) or a critical edition, never from this file.

The 1651 'Life of Agrippa' says he was famous 'about 1530' and then 'gave his minde to writing, and composed three Books Of Occult Philosophy'. That puts the books after 1530, which Agrippa's own prefaces and the 1510 letters contradict. Do not follow the Life.

CROSS-CHECK (trithemius sibling): the TCP wording of Trithemius's advice is 'Yet this one rule I advise you to observe, that you communicate vulgar secrets to vulgar friends, but higher and secret to higher, and secret friends only. Give Hey to an Ox, Sugar to a Parret only; understand my meaning, least you be trod under the Oxens feet, as oftentimes it fals out.' The sibling's 'Give hay to an Ox, sugar to a Parrot' is a modernised form.

CROSS-CHECK (planetary-seals sibling): the TCP keying of II.22 reads 'with an Intelligency to what is good, with a spirit to what is bad' (not 'Intelligence ... Spirit'). Its Saturn, Jupiter, Mars and Sun squares agree cell for cell with the sibling's layouts (checked by script). Its Venus, Mercury and Moon squares differ from the sibling's in several cells: 1651 misprints (its errata correct numbers on pp. 247, 249 and 251) and illegible cells. So the 1651 cannot confirm those three; use the 1533 plates.
